titleStmt.title: Money Priming Can Change People’s Thoughts, Feelings, Motivations, and Behaviors: An Update on 10 Years of Experiments

bibl.title: Money Priming Can Change People’s Thoughts, Feelings, Motivations, and Behaviors: An Update on 10 Years of Experiments

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Variations in a prime’s meaning, the ease with which primed content comes to mind, the prime’s motivational importance, and the ambiguity of the outcome situation influence the impact of the prime.

span.label: money priming
span.quote: Money priming experiments (totaling 165 to date, from 18 countries) point to at least 2 major effects.

span.label: review
span.quote: This article discusses the factors that predict priming effects, and particularly those pertinent to differences between Caruso et al. and Rohrer et al.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Priming works by supplying an interpretation for an ambiguous outcome situation, so the more constrained and unambiguous the outcome, the less room the prime has to shift the response and the smaller the effect
span.quote: The more specific and less ambiguous the outcome (such as when responding to the word doctor after seeing the word nurse), the smaller the expected priming effect because there is less wiggle room for the prime to alter the response (e.g., Loersch & Payne, 2011).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Frequent real-world contact with money keeps the concept chronically accessible, so that even subtle cues suffice to activate it and change behaviour
span.quote: When the content of a prime is easily accessible, it can take only subtle cues reminiscent of it to alter outcomes (Higgins & Brendl, 1995).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Money cues set two opposing forces in motion - one routing from money to free markets to endorsement of the systems supporting them, the other routing from money to personal agency and self-sufficiency, which removes the need to endorse those systems - and the two cancel
span.quote: Integrating the two lines of reasoning suggests that there might be countervailing forces when people are primed with money and asked to contemplate the righteousness of existing social systems.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Money primes act by activating the phenomenological self as an owner of money, which is why primes tying money to the participant personally produce parallel and stronger effects
span.quote: Parallels between general money prime effects and primes that highlight the self owning money suggest that self activation might be an important contributor.

span.label: The review is explicitly partial: it does not cover the full body of money-priming experiments.
span.quote: I did not have the space to cover the entirety of money priming experiments, which are 165 at last count.

span.label: The author's own proposed mediator (independence/interdependence) was only weakly supported.
span.quote: Scores were in the predicted direction, but only weakly.

span.label: The originally hypothesised mechanism, feelings of power, was not supported by the authors' own measurements.
span.quote: We measured feelings of power multiple times using a published scale (Schmidt & Frieze, 1997) as well as items we created but did not see changes in power as a result of money priming.

span.label: money priming
span.quote: Thus began our investigation of whether money priming could alter responses related to system justification, social dominance, belief in a just world, and free market ideology

span.label: ambiguity
span.quote: Ambiguity of the outcome variable determines when and why primes exert their effects (Higgins & Brendl, 1995; Loersch & Payne, 2011)

span.label: priming effect
span.quote: A situation that does not leave much room for interpretation is unlikely to show a consistent or large priming effect

span.label: accessibility
span.quote: Another factor that renders primes more or less influential is accessibility, which is related to experience and motivational relevance

span.label: system justification
span.quote: Thus began our investigation of whether money priming could alter responses related to system justification, social dominance, belief in a just world, and free market ideology

span.label: A THEORY OF WHEN PRIMING WORKS AT ALL, OFFERED IN REPLY TO A FAILED REPLICATION. `Variations in a prime's MEANING, the EASE with which primed content comes to mind, the prime's MOTIVATIONAL IMPORTANCE, and the AMBIGUITY OF THE OUTCOME SITUATION influence the impact of the prime.` Four moderators, stated in the abstract of a paper whose third sentence is that Rohrer, Pashler and Harris failed to replicate. **The provenance matters as much as the content**: these are conditions named AFTER a null, which is the weakest position from which to name them and also the position in which the field most needs them named
span.quote: Variations in a prime’s meaning, the ease with which primed content comes to mind, the prime’s motivational importance, and the ambiguity of the outcome situation influence the impact of the prime

span.label: AMBIGUITY OF THE OUTCOME IS OFFERED AS THE REASON COGNITIVE PRIMING EFFECTS ARE SMALLER THAN SOCIAL ONES, WHICH INVERTS THE USUAL READING. `The more specific and LESS AMBIGUOUS the outcome (such as when responding to the word doctor after seeing the word nurse), THE SMALLER the expected priming effect because there is less wiggle room for the prime to alter the response.` The usual account of that same effect-size gap is that social priming effects are inflated. This says they are large because the outcome is loose - a property of the MEASURE, not of the phenomenon - and it makes the gap a prediction rather than an embarrassment. **Both readings fit the same numbers, and this corpus holds papers from both sides of the gap**
span.quote: The more specific and less ambiguous the outcome (such as when responding to the word doctor after seeing the word nurse), the smaller the expected priming effect because there is less wiggle room for the prime to alter the response

span.label: AND IT IS FALSIFIABLE, WITH THE TEST SUPPLIED: `A situation that does not leave much room for interpretation IS UNLIKELY TO SHOW A CONSISTENT OR LARGE PRIMING EFFECT.` The same outcome task was given two NAMES - Kay et al. (2004) called it either a bland `situation` or a `community game` - and `business priming led to more competitive behaviors than neutral primes when the task was blandly called a situation, THERE WAS NO EFFECT of prime condition when the task was called the community game`. **Ambiguity manipulated by renaming, with a null in the constrained arm.** That is a much stronger form of the claim than a post-hoc moderator, and it is the paper's best evidence
span.quote: Whereas business priming led to more competitive behaviors than neutral primes when the task was blandly called a “situation,” there was no effect of prime condition when the task was called the “community game

span.label: THE PAPER'S OWN SUMMARY OF 165 EXPERIMENTS IS TWO EFFECTS, BOTH STATED AS DIRECTIONS RATHER THAN SIZES: people reminded of money `are LESS INTERPERSONALLY ATTUNED. They are not prosocial, caring, or warm. They eschew interdependence.` And they `shift into professional, business, and work mentality. They exert effort on challenging tasks, demonstrate good performance, and feel efficacious.` A count that large (`165 to date, from 18 countries`) with no pooled effect size is itself a fact about the literature - the defence is breadth of replication rather than magnitude
span.quote: Money priming experiments (totaling 165 to date, from 18 countries) point to at least 2 major effects. First, compared to neutral primes, people reminded of money are less interpersonally attuned. They are not prosocial, caring, or warm. They eschew interdependence. Second, people reminded of money shift into professional, business, and work mentality. They exert effort on challenging tasks, demonstrate good performance, and feel efficacious

span.label: builds-on → Caruso, Vohs, Baxter, and Waytz (2013)
span.quote: Thus began our investigation of whether money priming could alter responses related to system justification, social dominance, belief in a just world, and free market ideology.

span.label: contradicts → Rohrer, Pashler, and Harris (2015)
span.quote: In summary, there are two theoretically derived reasons why Rohrer et al.’s (2015) results were inconsistent with Caruso et al.’s (2013).

span.label: ambiguity —causes→ priming effect
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE DIRECTION IS STATED AS ITS CONTRAPOSITIVE - less room, smaller effect - and the axis quote carries it that way rather than being paraphrased into the positive form. Weight 0.85: the first clause is cited to Higgins & Brendl and Loersch & Payne rather than demonstrated here, and this paper's own status is a reply to a null. The Kay et al. manipulation is the evidence, and it is in the senses.
span.quote: Ambiguity of the outcome variable determines when and why primes exert their effects (Higgins & Brendl, 1995; Loersch & Payne, 2011). A situation that does not leave much room for interpretation is unlikely to show a consistent or large priming effect

span.label: money priming —causes→ system justification
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — **WEIGHT 0.6, AND IT IS THE CONTESTED CLAIM ITSELF.** The span is the hypothesis - `whether money priming COULD alter` - not a result, and it is deliberately the hypothesis: this is the exact effect that Rohrer, Pashler and Harris (2015) FAILED TO REPLICATE, which the paper states in its own abstract. No `effect_direction`: an edge asserting a direction here would take a side in a live dispute that the record's own claim_relations already document from both ends.
span.quote: Thus began our investigation of whether money priming could alter responses related to system justification, social dominance, belief in a just world, and free market ideology

span.label: effect size (Cohen's d)
span.quote: Effects of Money Priming on Performance Measures Following Vohs et al. (2006) Experiment Country Sample characteristics Manipulation Dependent measure N dmoney vs. neutral

span.label: sample size
span.quote: Note. Effects in bold are replications of Vohs et al. (2006).

span.label: Across the accumulated money-priming literature the author identifies two robust effects: reduced interpersonal attunement, and a shift into a work and business mentality.
span.quote: Money priming experiments (totaling 165 to date, from 18 countries) point to at least 2 major effects.

span.label: People reminded of money become less prosocial, less caring and less warm, and avoid interdependence.
span.quote: First, compared to neutral primes, people reminded of money are less interpersonally attuned.

span.label: People reminded of money work harder on difficult tasks, perform better on objective outcomes, and report feeling efficacious.
span.quote: They exert effort on challenging tasks, demonstrate good performance, and feel efficacious.

span.label: Feelings of power were tested repeatedly as the explanation for money-priming effects and were not supported: money primes did not change measured power.
span.quote: We measured feelings of power multiple times using a published scale (Schmidt & Frieze, 1997) as well as items we created but did not see changes in power as a result of money priming.

span.label: The independence-interdependence self-construal account fared only marginally better: scores moved in the predicted direction but only weakly.
span.quote: Scores were in the predicted direction, but only weakly.

span.label: The sign of the effect depends on how the money is presented: new or clean money increases moral, fair and prosocial responding, whereas used or dirty money produces greed and exploitation.
span.quote: Compared to used money or neutral primes, people reminded of new money make more moral decisions, think of themselves as prosocial and act accordingly, seek to be fair, and think about honesty and fair dealings.

span.label: Money priming is not interchangeable with priming other means of exchange: credit card cues loosen spending constraints while cash cues sharpen attention to price and cost.
span.quote: Cash cues, in contrast, heighten sensitivity to costs, as seen in more paying attention to price, reduced desire to spend, and a broad motivation to avoid mistakes (Chatterjee et al., 2013; Chatterjee & Rose, 2012; Mandel & Johnson, 2002; Tong et al., 2013).

span.label: The same pattern of effects appears in undergraduates, working adults, managers and children as young as four, across North America, Europe and Asia.
span.quote: College students, working adults, children as young as 4 years old, and business managers show similar effects (Tables 1 and 2; for a fuller review of the experiments to date [165 and counting], see Baumeister & Vohs, 2015).

span.label: Different delivery methods for the money prime - images, physical handling, even play money - yield comparable effects.
span.quote: Viewing images of money, touching money, and even seeing or holding play money can produce similar effects

span.label: Primes that link the money to the participant's own holdings, such as withdrawing cash from a machine or thinking about one's own wages, cut helpfulness and volunteering, suggesting self-relevance strengthens the effect.
span.quote: Two field studies in France showed that getting money out of a cash machine (and thus being reminded of one’s own money) reduced behavioral helpfulness more than walking by a cash dispenser (Guéguen & Jacob, 2013).

span.label: The proposed reason the Caruso et al. system-justification result failed to replicate is that money priming induces self-sufficiency, which works against the defensive motive that normally drives system justification.
span.quote: Money primes stimulate a sense that one can survive and thrive on one’s own, which might quell a defensive need to bolster the existing systems.

span.label: A second proposed reason for the replication discrepancy is sample-specific meaning of money: Caruso et al.'s University of Chicago and 2011 Mechanical Turk participants plausibly held a tighter, more favourable link between money and free-market systems than later samples.
span.quote: Rohrer, Pashler, and Harris (2015) failed to replicate those effects.

span.label: exchange mentality
span.quote: Money priming brings to mind an exchange mentality, in which people consider what they are giving up for what they will get in return (Jiang, Chen, & Wyer, 2014).

span.label: independence and interdependence (self-construal)
span.quote: Another hypothesis was that, tracking the behavioral outcomes we were observing, money primes would shift scores on a scale measuring independence (seeing the self as unique and separate from others) and interdependence (seeing the self as similar to others and socially connected; Singelis, 1994).

span.label: low control
span.quote: When people feel they cannot effectively bring about desired outcomes (a state of low control), they endorse social systems as a way to compensate (as reviewed by Kay & Friesen, 2011).

span.label: money prime versus neutral prime
span.quote: Hence, the authors predicted that money primes would boost system justification, social dominance, belief in a just world, and free market ideology, and found supportive evidence.

span.label: whose money is brought to mind (one's own wages versus others' wages)
span.term: whose money is brought to mind (one's own wages versus others' wages)
span.quote: Pfeffer and Devoe (2009) instructed people to think about their own, as opposed to others’, wages.

span.label: feelings of power
span.quote: We predicted that feeling more powerful than otherwise was a likely candidate to explain money priming effects.

span.label: independence-interdependence self-construal scores
span.quote: Another hypothesis was that, tracking the behavioral outcomes we were observing, money primes would shift scores on a scale measuring independence (seeing the self as unique and separate from others) and interdependence (seeing the self as similar to others and socially connected; Singelis, 1994).

span.label: ambiguity of the outcome situation
span.quote: Variations in a prime’s meaning, the ease with which primed content comes to mind, the prime’s motivational importance, and the ambiguity of the outcome situation influence the impact of the prime.

span.label: accessibility and motivational importance of the primed content
span.term: accessibility and motivational importance of the primed content
span.quote: Another factor that renders primes more or less influential is accessibility, which is related to experience and motivational relevance.

span.label: 165 — total number of money-priming experiments counted to date, run in 18 countries
span.quote: Money priming experiments (totaling 165 to date, from 18 countries) point to at least 2 major effects.

span.label: 200% — increase in intended donations produced by a credit card prime relative to no prime
span.quote: A credit card prime, compared to a no prime condition, led to a 200% increase in intended donations in a laboratory experiment (Feinberg, 1986).

span.label: 113% — increase in bids in a real binding auction for a credit card prime versus a cash prime
span.quote: A credit card prime, versus cash, led to a 113% percent increase in a real, binding auction (Prelec & Simester, 2001).
